questions.q: Why does a monopolist's MR curve lie below its AR curve?
options: It must lower its price on all units to sell one more
It pays a tax on each unit
questions.why: Cutting the price to sell more means earning less on the units it could have sold for more.

questions.q: A monopolist sells {q} units at £{p}. Its ATC at that output is £{a}. What is its abnormal profit, in £?
Match each case to the source of its monopoly power.
pairs: A drug firm holds the only legal right to make a medicine
Only one firm sells in a town
A firm spends heavily on adverts
Customers see a brand as unique
questions.why: Each of these makes demand less elastic or keeps rivals out.

questions.q: Compared with where P = MC, a monopolist produces:
options: Less output at a higher price
More output at a higher price
Less output at a lower price
The same output at the same price
questions.why: The monopolist restricts output so that it can charge more.

questions.q: Firms in oligopoly and monopolistic competition are also price makers.
questions.why: They have varying degrees of monopoly power.

questions.q: Which is a possible benefit of monopoly for consumers?
options: Prices can be lower if economies of scale are large
Output is always above the competitive level
The firm has no reason to make a profit
questions.why: Large enough cost savings can mean a lower price than many small firms would charge.

questions.q: Explain why a monopolist can keep making abnormal profit in the long run.

ideas.label: Barriers to entry stop new firms from entering
So supply doesn't rise and the price isn't competed down

questions.model: Barriers to entry stop new firms from entering the market, so there is no competition to undercut the monopolist and push the price down.
questions.why: Without entry, nothing competes the profit away.

tests.answer: Barriers to entry stop new firms entering, so there is no competition to push prices down.
